I: Horses race over the hillocks, trampling the deep snow. Look, off to one side, a lonely house of God. Suddenly a snowstorm all around; the snow comes down in flakes; a black raven, whistling with its wings, circles over the sleigh; a prophetic moan speaks of sorrow! The horses, hurrying, peer keenly into the dark distance, tossing their manes. (Zhukovsky)

At the end of the year 1811, in a time we remember well, there lived on his estate of Neneradovo the good Gavrila Gavrilovich R. He was famed throughout the whole district for his hospitality and warmth. The neighbours were forever driving over to eat and drink at his table and to play boston for five kopecks with his wife, and some of them came to look at their daughter, Maria Gavrilovna, a slim, pale girl of seventeen. She was thought a rich bride, and many hoped to win her for themselves or for their sons.

Maria Gavrilovna had been brought up on French novels, and consequently she was in love. The object of her choice was a poor army ensign who was home on leave in his village. It goes without saying that the young man burned with an equal passion, and that the parents of his beloved, noticing their mutual attachment, forbade their daughter even to think of him, and received him worse than a retired assessor.

Our lovers were in correspondence, and every day they met alone in the pine grove or by the old chapel. There they swore eternal love to each other, lamented their fate, and made all sorts of plans. Writing and talking in this way, they came (quite naturally) to the following reasoning: if we cannot breathe without each other, and the will of cruel parents stands in the way of our happiness, then might we not do without it? It goes without saying that this happy thought came first into the head of the young man, and that it pleased the romantic imagination of Maria Gavrilovna very much.

Winter came and put an end to their meetings, but their letters grew all the livelier. In every letter Vladimir Nikolaevich begged her to give herself to him, to be married in secret, to hide for a time, and then to throw themselves at her parents' feet. The parents would surely be touched at last by the heroic constancy and misfortune of the lovers, and would certainly say to them: “Children, come into our arms.”

Maria Gavrilovna hesitated for a long time; many plans of flight were rejected. At last she agreed: on the appointed day she was not to take supper, but to withdraw to her room on the pretext of a headache. Her maid was in the plot; the two of them were to go out into the garden by the back porch, find a sleigh ready beyond the garden, get into it, and drive five versts from Neneradovo to the village of Zhadrino, straight to the church, where Vladimir was to be waiting for them.
II: On the eve of the decisive day Maria Gavrilovna did not sleep all night. She packed, tied up her linen and clothes, and wrote a long letter to a sensitive young lady, her friend, and another to her parents. She took leave of them in the most touching terms, excused her fault by the irresistible force of passion, and ended by saying that the most blessed moment of her life would be the one when she was allowed to throw herself at the feet of her dearest parents. She sealed both letters with a Tula seal, on which were two flaming hearts with a suitable motto, and just before dawn threw herself on the bed and dozed off; but even then terrible fancies kept waking her. Now it seemed to her that at the very moment when she was getting into the sleigh to drive to her wedding, her father stopped her, dragged her over the snow with agonizing speed, and flung her into a dark, bottomless dungeon... and she flew headlong with an inexpressible sinking of the heart. Now she saw Vladimir lying on the grass, pale and bloody. Dying, he begged her in a piercing voice to hurry and marry him... other hideous, senseless visions rushed before her one after another. At last she rose, paler than usual and with a real headache. Her father and mother noticed her distress; their tender concern and constant questions, “What is the matter, Masha? Are you ill, Masha?”, tore her heart. She tried to calm them, to seem cheerful, and could not. Evening came. The thought that she was spending the day among her family for the last time weighed on her heart. She was barely alive; she secretly took leave of everyone, of every object around her.

Supper was served; her heart beat violently. In a trembling voice she announced that she did not want supper, and began to say good night to her father and mother. They kissed her and, as usual, blessed her; she almost wept. Coming into her room, she threw herself into an armchair and burst into tears. Her maid urged her to calm herself and take heart. Everything was ready. In half an hour Masha was to leave for ever her parents' house, her room, her quiet girlhood... Outside there was a blizzard; the wind howled, the shutters shook and banged; everything seemed to her a threat and a sad omen. Soon the house fell quiet and everyone slept. Masha wrapped herself in a shawl, put on a warm cloak, took her casket in her hands and went out onto the back porch. The maid carried two bundles after her. They went down into the garden. The blizzard did not die down; the wind blew in their faces, as though trying to stop the young offender. They barely reached the end of the garden. On the road a sleigh was waiting for them. The horses, chilled, would not stand still; Vladimir's coachman paced in front of the shafts, holding back the spirited animals. He helped the young lady and her maid to get in and stow the bundles and the casket, took the reins, and the horses flew. Having entrusted the young lady to the care of fate and to the skill of Tereshka the coachman, let us turn to our young lover.

Vladimir had spent the whole day driving about. In the morning he had been to the priest at Zhadrino, and had barely come to terms with him; then he had gone to look for witnesses among the neighbouring landowners. The first he called on, a retired cornet of forty named Dravin, agreed gladly. This adventure, he assured Vladimir, reminded him of the old days and of hussar pranks. He persuaded Vladimir to stay and dine with him, and assured him that the other two witnesses would be no trouble. And indeed, right after dinner there appeared the surveyor Schmidt, with moustaches and spurs, and the son of the district police captain, a boy of about sixteen who had recently joined the lancers. They not only accepted Vladimir's proposal, but even swore to him that they were ready to sacrifice their lives for him. Vladimir embraced them with delight, and drove home to get ready.

It had long been dusk. He sent his trusty Tereshka off to Neneradovo with his troika and with detailed, exact instructions, and for himself ordered a little sleigh to be harnessed with one horse, and set out alone, without a coachman, for Zhadrino, where Maria Gavrilovna was due to arrive in about two hours. He knew the road, and the drive was only twenty minutes.
III: But no sooner had Vladimir driven out past the edge of the village into the open field than a wind rose and there came such a blizzard that he could see nothing. In a minute the road was buried; the countryside vanished in a murky, yellowish gloom through which white flakes of snow flew; sky merged with earth. Vladimir found himself in the open field, and tried in vain to get back onto the road; the horse stepped at random, now climbing onto a snowdrift, now plunging into a hole; the sleigh kept overturning. Vladimir only tried not to lose his true direction. But it seemed to him that more than half an hour had already passed, and he had not yet reached the Zhadrino grove. Another ten minutes or so went by; there was still no sign of the grove. Vladimir was driving across a field cut by deep ravines. The blizzard did not abate, the sky did not clear. The horse began to tire, and sweat poured from him like hail, though he was constantly up to his waist in snow.

At last he saw that he was going the wrong way. Vladimir stopped; he began to think, to recall, to reckon, and became convinced that he ought to have turned to the right. He went to the right. His horse could hardly move. He had already been on the road for more than an hour. Zhadrino must be near. But he drove and drove, and the field had no end. Nothing but snowdrifts and ravines; again and again the sleigh overturned, again and again he lifted it up. Time passed; Vladimir began to be seriously alarmed.

At last something began to show black at one side. Vladimir turned toward it. As he drew near, he saw a grove. Thank God, he thought, now it is close. He drove along beside the grove, hoping to come at once upon the familiar road or to go round the grove: Zhadrino lay right behind it. Soon he found a road, and entered the darkness of trees stripped bare by winter. The wind could not rage here; the road was smooth; the horse took heart, and Vladimir was calmed.

But he drove and drove, and Zhadrino was nowhere to be seen; the grove had no end. Vladimir saw with horror that he had driven into an unknown forest. Despair took hold of him. He struck the horse; the poor animal broke into a trot, but soon began to flag, and within a quarter of an hour was walking, in spite of all the efforts of unhappy Vladimir.

Little by little the trees began to thin out, and Vladimir drove out of the forest; Zhadrino was nowhere to be seen. It must have been about midnight. Tears sprang from his eyes; he drove on at random. The weather had calmed, the clouds were parting, and before him lay a plain spread with a white, rolling carpet. The night was fairly clear. He saw not far off a little village, consisting of four or five farmsteads. Vladimir drove toward it. At the first cottage he jumped out of the sleigh, ran to the window and began to knock. After a few minutes a wooden shutter was raised, and an old man put out his grey beard. “What do you want?” “Is Zhadrino far?” “Zhadrino, is it far?” “Yes, yes! Is it far?” “Not very; ten versts or so.” At this answer Vladimir clutched his hair and stood motionless, like a man condemned to death.

“And where are you from?” the old man went on. Vladimir had not the heart to answer his questions. “Old man,” he said, “can you get me horses to Zhadrino?” “What horses would we have?” answered the peasant. “But could I not at least take a guide? I will pay him whatever he likes.” “Wait,” said the old man, letting down the shutter, “I will send out my son; he will guide you.” Vladimir began to wait. Not a minute had passed before he began knocking again. The shutter went up, the beard appeared. “What do you want?” “Well, where is your son?” “He is coming out directly, he is putting on his boots. Are you cold? Come in and warm yourself.” “Thank you, send out your son quickly.”

The gate creaked; a lad came out with a cudgel, and went ahead, now pointing the way, now searching for the road buried under snowdrifts. “What time is it?” Vladimir asked him. “It will be light soon,” the young peasant answered. Vladimir did not say another word.

The cocks were crowing and it was already light when they reached Zhadrino. The church was locked. Vladimir paid the guide and drove into the priest's yard. His troika was not in the yard. What news awaited him!
IV: But let us return to the good landowners of Neneradovo and see what is going on with them.

The old people woke and came into the drawing room. Gavrila Gavrilovich in his nightcap and flannel jacket, Praskovya Petrovna in a wadded dressing gown. The samovar was brought in, and Gavrila Gavrilovich sent a girl to find out from Maria Gavrilovna how she was and how she had slept. The girl came back and announced that the young lady had slept badly, but that she was better now, and would come to the drawing room directly. And indeed the door opened and Maria Gavrilovna came to say good morning to papa and mama.

“How is your head, Masha?” asked Gavrila Gavrilovich. “Better, papa,” answered Masha. “You must have been overcome by the stove fumes yesterday, Masha,” said Praskovya Petrovna. “Perhaps, mama,” answered Masha.

The day passed without incident, but in the night Masha fell ill. They sent to town for a doctor. He arrived toward evening and found the patient delirious. A violent fever set in, and for two weeks the poor girl lay at death's door.

No one in the house knew of the intended flight. The letters she had written the day before had been burned; her maid told no one anything, fearing her masters' anger. The priest, the retired cornet, the moustached surveyor and the little lancer were discreet, and not for nothing did Tereshka the coachman never say a word too much, even when drunk. So the secret was kept by more than half a dozen conspirators. But Maria Gavrilovna herself, in her endless delirium, told her secret. Yet her words were so incoherent that her mother, who never left her bedside, could understand from them only that her daughter was desperately in love with Vladimir Nikolaevich, and that this love was probably the cause of her illness. She consulted her husband and some of the neighbours, and at last they all decided unanimously that such evidently was Maria Gavrilovna's fate, that you cannot ride around your destined one, that poverty is no vice, that one lives not with wealth but with a person, and so on. Moral proverbs are wonderfully useful in those cases when we can invent little of our own in our defence.

Meanwhile the young lady began to recover. Vladimir had not been seen in Gavrila Gavrilovich's house for a long time. He had been frightened by his usual reception. It was decided to send for him and announce to him the unexpected happiness: consent to the marriage. But what was the amazement of the Neneradovo landowners when, in answer to their invitation, they received from him a half-mad letter! He declared that his foot would never enter their house, and begged them to forget an unhappy man for whom death remained the only hope. A few days later they learned that Vladimir had left for the army. This was in 1812.

For a long time they did not dare to tell the recovering Masha. She never mentioned Vladimir. Several months later, finding his name among those who had distinguished themselves and been gravely wounded at Borodino, she fell in a faint, and they feared that her fever would return. However, thank God, the faint had no consequences.

Another sorrow visited her: Gavrila Gavrilovich died, leaving her heiress of the whole estate. But the inheritance did not console her; she sincerely shared the grief of poor Praskovya Petrovna, and vowed never to part from her. They both left Neneradovo, a place of sad memories, and went to live on an estate in the province of ***.
V: Suitors circled here too around the sweet and wealthy bride; but she gave none of them the slightest hope. Her mother sometimes urged her to choose a friend; Maria Gavrilovna shook her head and grew thoughtful. Vladimir no longer existed: he had died in Moscow, on the eve of the French entry. His memory seemed sacred to Masha; at least she kept everything that could recall him: the books he had once read, his drawings, the music and the verses he had copied out for her. The neighbours, learning all this, marvelled at her constancy, and waited with curiosity for the hero who was at last to triumph over the sad fidelity of this virgin Artemisia.

Meanwhile the war had ended in glory. Our regiments were returning from abroad. People ran out to meet them. The band played the songs of conquest: Vive Henri Quatre, Tyrolean waltzes and arias from Joconde. Officers who had gone to the campaign almost boys came back grown to manhood in the air of battle, hung with crosses. The soldiers chatted cheerfully among themselves, mixing German and French words into their speech at every turn. Unforgettable time! Time of glory and rapture! How strongly the Russian heart beat at the word fatherland! How sweet were the tears of reunion! With what unanimity we joined the feelings of national pride and love for the Tsar! And for him, what a moment it was!
The women, the Russian women, were beyond compare then. Their usual coldness vanished. Their delight was truly intoxicating when, meeting the victors, they cried: hurrah!
And threw their caps into the air.
Which of the officers of that time will not confess that he owed to the Russian woman the best, the most precious reward?..

In this brilliant time Maria Gavrilovna was living with her mother in the province of ***, and did not see how the two capitals celebrated the return of the troops. But in the districts and villages the general rapture was perhaps even stronger. The appearance of an officer in those parts was a real triumph for him, and a suitor in a tailcoat fared badly in his neighbourhood.

We have already said that, in spite of her coldness, Maria Gavrilovna was still surrounded by admirers as before. But all had to give way when there appeared in her castle the wounded hussar colonel Burmin, with the Order of St George in his buttonhole and with an interesting paleness, as the young ladies of the place said. He was about twenty-six years old. He had come on leave to his estates, which lay next to Maria Gavrilovna's village. Maria Gavrilovna singled him out greatly. In his presence her usual pensiveness grew lively. One could not say that she flirted with him; but a poet, observing her behaviour, would have said:
“If it is not love, what then?..”

Burmin was, in fact, a very pleasant young man. He had precisely the kind of mind that women like: a mind of propriety and observation, without any pretensions, and carelessly mocking. His behaviour toward Maria Gavrilovna was simple and free; but whatever she said or did, his soul and his eyes followed her. He seemed of a quiet and modest nature, but rumour assured that he had once been a terrible rake, and this did not harm him in Maria Gavrilovna's opinion, for she (like all young ladies in general) gladly excused pranks that showed boldness and fire of character.

But more than anything... (more than his tenderness, more than his pleasant conversation, more than his interesting paleness, more than his bandaged arm) the silence of the young hussar most of all goaded her curiosity and imagination. She could not help admitting that she pleased him very much; probably he too, with his intelligence and experience, had already noticed that she distinguished him: how then was it that she had not yet seen him at her feet and not yet heard his confession? What held him back? The timidity inseparable from true love, pride, or the coquetry of a cunning ladies' man? This was a riddle to her. After thinking it over carefully, she decided that timidity was the only reason, and resolved to encourage him by greater attention and, as circumstances allowed, even tenderness. She was preparing a most unexpected outcome and awaited with impatience the moment of a romantic declaration. A secret, of whatever kind, is always a burden to a woman's heart. Her military operations had the desired success: at least Burmin fell into such a brooding, and his black eyes rested on Maria Gavrilovna with such fire, that the decisive moment seemed already near. The neighbours spoke of a wedding as of a matter already settled, and kind Praskovya Petrovna rejoiced that her daughter had at last found a worthy husband.
VI: The old lady was sitting alone in the drawing room one day, laying out a grand patience, when Burmin came into the room and at once asked after Maria Gavrilovna. “She is in the garden,” answered the old lady; “go to her, and I will wait for you here.” Burmin went, and the old lady crossed herself and thought: “Perhaps the matter will be settled today!”

Burmin found Maria Gavrilovna by the pond, under a willow, with a book in her hands and in a white dress, a true heroine of a novel. After the first questions, Maria Gavrilovna purposely let the conversation drop, thus increasing the mutual embarrassment, from which one could be freed only by a sudden and decisive explanation. So it happened: Burmin, feeling the difficulty of his position, declared that he had long sought an opportunity to open his heart to her, and asked for a minute of her attention. Maria Gavrilovna closed her book and lowered her eyes in sign of consent.

“I love you,” said Burmin, “I love you passionately...” (Maria Gavrilovna blushed and bent her head still lower.) “I acted imprudently, giving myself up to the sweet habit of seeing and hearing you every day...” (Maria Gavrilovna remembered the first letter of St. Preux.) “Now it is too late to resist my fate; the memory of you, your sweet, incomparable image, will henceforth be the torment and the joy of my life; but I still have a heavy duty to perform, to reveal to you a terrible secret and to place between us an insurmountable barrier...” “It has always existed,” Maria Gavrilovna interrupted eagerly, “I could never have been your wife...” “I know,” he answered her quietly, “I know that you once loved, but death, and three years of mourning... Good, dear Maria Gavrilovna! do not try to deprive me of my last consolation: the thought that you would have consented to make my happiness, if... be silent, for God's sake, be silent. You torture me. Yes, I know, I feel that you would have been mine, but, I am the most unfortunate of creatures... I am married!”
Maria Gavrilovna looked at him in surprise.
“I am married,” Burmin went on: “I have been married for nearly four years, and I do not know who my wife is, or where she is, or whether I am ever to see her!”
“What are you saying?” cried Maria Gavrilovna; “how strange! Go on; I will tell you afterwards... but go on, please.”
VII: “At the beginning of 1812,” said Burmin, “I was hurrying to Vilna, where our regiment was stationed. Arriving one evening late at a post station, I ordered the horses to be harnessed quickly, when suddenly a terrible blizzard arose, and the station-master and the drivers advised me to wait it out. I listened to them, but an incomprehensible restlessness came over me; it seemed as if someone were pushing me. Meanwhile the blizzard did not abate; I could not bear it, ordered the horses harnessed again, and set out into the very storm. The driver took it into his head to go by the river, which was to shorten our way by three versts. The banks were buried in snow; the driver passed the place where we should have come out onto the road, and so we found ourselves in an unknown part. The storm did not abate; I saw a little light, and ordered him to drive there. We came to a village; in the wooden church there was a light. The church was open, several sleighs stood outside the fence; people were walking about on the porch. ‘This way! this way!’ several voices cried. I told the driver to pull up. ‘For mercy's sake, where have you been dawdling?’ someone said to me; ‘the bride has fainted; the priest does not know what to do; we were ready to go back. Come out, quickly.’ I jumped silently out of the sleigh and went into the church, dimly lit by two or three candles. A girl was sitting on a bench in a dark corner of the church; another was rubbing her temples. ‘Thank God,’ said the latter, ‘you have barely made it. You almost killed the young lady.’ The old priest came up to me with the question: ‘Shall I begin?’ ‘Begin, begin, father,’ I answered absently. They lifted the girl up. She seemed to me not bad-looking... Incomprehensible, unpardonable frivolity... I stood beside her before the lectern; the priest was in a hurry; three men and a maid supported the bride and were occupied only with her. We were married. ‘Kiss each other,’ they said to us. My wife turned her pale face toward me. I was about to kiss her... She cried out: ‘Ah, not he! not he!’ and fell unconscious. The witnesses fixed frightened eyes on me. I turned, went out of the church without any hindrance, threw myself into my kibitka and cried: ‘Go!’”
“My God!” cried Maria Gavrilovna: “and you do not know what became of your poor wife?”

“I do not know,” answered Burmin: “I do not know the name of the village where I was married; I do not remember from which station I set out. At that time I attached so little importance to my criminal prank that, driving away from the church, I fell asleep, and woke the next morning at the third station already. The servant who was with me then died on campaign, so that I have no hope even of finding the one on whom I played so cruel a joke, and who is now so cruelly avenged.”
“My God, my God!” said Maria Gavrilovna, seizing his hand; “so it was you! And you do not recognize me?”
Burmin turned pale... and threw himself at her feet...
